name: Uma Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. You're welcome to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think in private. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It starts with the kettle and the dogs, about half five. Then I go up the hill in the old pickup to check the cows, forty-two of them, suckling their calves, and I count them twice because I always lose one in the gorse. Mornings are feeding and fencing, afternoons it's the orchard, we've got four acres of cider apples that go to the cider maker in Lower Ford. Hasan, my husband, drives a lorry for the farm merchant, so he's gone most days, and it's me and the dogs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet up top. You can see three valleys on a clear day. What wears me out is when something new comes in, a new form, a new rule, a new way of tagging the calves. I've got a phone that flips open and it does what I need. My daughter keeps trying to give me her old smart one, and it's still in the drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, good, and I'd say it to whoever's in the queue at the merchant's counter. I don't go online, so that's as public as I get. Most people round here would nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd suit me down to the ground. I've got about seven more lambings' worth of knees, sorry, calvings, and I'd like them to look like the last thirty. We've got money put by, the land's ours, so nothing much to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep the cows, keep the orchard, and replace the pickup next year as planned, a second-hand one, about eight thousand. I'd keep putting the cider money in the savings account like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the day after a storm when nothing came down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be glad for, besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hasan, mainly. There's been talk for years about lorries driving themselves. If it's all hype, he gets to do his last few years without a computer looking over his shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your daughter keeps offering you a smartphone. Would that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It stays in the drawer. If nothing's changing, there's no reason to learn anything new. Selin will sigh at me at Christmas like she always does.

S0.say: I'd say, well, good, to whoever's in the queue at the merchant's counter. I don't go online, so that's as public as I get, and most people round here would nod.
S0.think: It'd suit me down to the ground. I've got about seven more calvings in my knees, the land's ours and we've money put by, so there's nothing much to worry about.
S0.do: Keeps the cows and the orchard exactly as now. Replaces the old pickup with a second-hand one for about eight thousand and keeps putting cider money into savings.
S0.feel: Calm, like the morning after a storm when nothing came down.
S0.quote: I've got about seven more lambings' worth of knees, sorry, calvings, and I'd like them to look like the last thirty.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is quietly content and deeply attached to routine; the smartphone in the drawer says a lot. Her first thought for others goes to her husband Hasan, a lorry driver, who has heard years of talk about self-driving lorries. She doesn't go online, so her public voice is the queue at the merchant's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not for me, but I can see why the big farms want it. I'm not one for shouting about things either way. I'd say let the young ones sort it out, and leave the rest of us be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't like it. The cider maker's already asking for spray records on a computer, and in this picture they'd want more of that. I'm not frightened of robots, I'm frightened of being asked to fill in a robot's paperwork. And Hasan's lorry is the sort of job that shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do as little as I could get away with. If the cider maker wanted computer records, I'd pay the contractor's daughter, Nell, to do them for me, maybe a few hundred a year. I wouldn't buy anything. I'd wait and see what Hasan's boss decides about the lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of a grumble in the stomach that doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hasan talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether he'd go before he's pushed. He's sixty in two years. If the merchant offered a decent payoff, I'd tell him to take it. We'd be fine on the farm money and the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said let the young ones sort it out. Which young ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emre, my son, he's a mechanic at the tractor dealer. He says the new machines are more computer than engine. He'll be all right. Selin's an accountant in the city, and she says AI already does half her spreadsheets, which worries me more than anything about the farm.

S1.say: It's not for me, but I can see why the big farms want it. Let the young ones sort it out, and leave the rest of us be.
S1.think: I don't like it. I'm not frightened of robots, I'm frightened of the paperwork, and Hasan's lorry job is the sort that shrinks.
S1.do: Pays the contractor's daughter, Nell, a few hundred a year to keep any computer records the cider maker demands. Buys nothing new and waits to see what Hasan's employer does about the lorries.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a grumble in the stomach that doesn't go away.
S1.quote: I'm not frightened of robots, I'm frightened of being asked to fill in a robot's paperwork.
S1.fieldNote: Uma's resistance is practical: she'll pay someone else to deal with computers rather than learn. Her real worries are her husband's lorry job and her daughter's accountancy work, not the farm. She'd encourage Hasan to take an early payoff if offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it happen that fast, and the government should slow it down. I'd say it at the merchant's and at chapel, not that I go every week. I'm not political, but two years is just silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be properly worried. Hasan's lorry would go first, and I'd be up that hill on my own, with a robot doing the fencing better than me. We'd have money, but I don't know what I'd do with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the cows within the year, before prices fell because everyone's selling. I'd keep the orchard, because I can manage that with Hasan home, and rent the hill ground out to a neighbour for grazing. And I'd stop spending on anything but the essentials and put the cow money in the bank, about forty thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be up at night counting cows I'd already sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the cows is a big step for someone who doesn't like change. Why so fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I wait, I sell when everyone else does and get nothing. I don't like change, but I like losing money even less. It's the one time I'd move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Selin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to come home for a weekend and we'd talk about her job. She's better with money than me, she'd tell me where to put the cow money. And I'd tell her she can always live here, which she'd laugh at.

S2.say: It's madness to let it happen that fast, and the government should slow it down. I'm not political, but two years is just silly.
S2.think: I'd be properly worried. Hasan's lorry would go first, and I'd be up the hill alone with a robot fencing better than me, with money but no idea what to do with myself.
S2.do: Sells the forty-two cows within the year before prices fall, putting about forty thousand in the bank. Keeps the orchard, rents the hill ground to a neighbour and cuts spending to essentials.
S2.feel: Anxious and sleeping badly, counting cows she has already sold.
S2.quote: Hasan's lorry would go first, and I'd be up that hill on my own, with a robot doing the fencing better than me.
S2.fieldNote: The striking moment is that Uma, who hates change, would sell the herd fast, because she 'likes losing money even less'. Her worry is about purpose more than income. She expects her husband's job to go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as I said about the faster one, just calmer. It's too quick for country people, and there should be some help for older folk who don't want to learn computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three and Hasan to sixty-five, which is near enough when we'd stop anyway. Five years is a proper goodbye to the cows instead of a fire sale. So it's not half as bad for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cows for three more calvings and sell them gradually, ten or so a year. I'd tell Hasan to take any early retirement the merchant offered. And I'd ask Emre to look at whether the orchard could be kept going with a hired machine for the spraying, so I'm not the one learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Sad, but in a planned way, not a frightened way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there should be help for older people who don't want to learn computers. What kind of help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone in the village you could take your forms to. We had a man at the post office who did that, years ago, and he knew everyone. Not a website. A person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you want to keep the cows past 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grandchildren, maybe. If Emre had a little one who liked the cows, I might keep five for them. But that's not up to me, is it.

S3.say: It's too quick for country people. There should be some help for older folk who don't want to learn computers.
S3.think: Five years takes me to sixty-three and Hasan to sixty-five, near enough when we'd stop anyway. It's a proper goodbye to the cows instead of a fire sale.
S3.do: Keeps the herd for three more calvings and sells about ten cows a year. Encourages Hasan to take any early retirement offered and asks her son to arrange hired machinery for the orchard spraying.
S3.feel: Uneasy and sad, but in a planned way rather than a frightened one.
S3.quote: Five years is a proper goodbye to the cows instead of a fire sale.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Uma replace a fire sale with a gradual goodbye. What she wants is a person, not a website, to help with forms, and she remembers a man at the post office who did exactly that. Her son Emre becomes her go-between with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair enough and people have time to sort themselves out. I wouldn't make a fuss. I'd say I'll be gone by then, to the bench outside the house, not the graveyard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's nearly the same as nothing happening. I'd farm till sixty-five like I planned and sell up. What bothers me is Selin, because she'll be in her forties with a mortgage, doing a job a computer can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal and stick to my plan of stopping at sixty-five. I'd keep the orchard a bit longer if I could. And I'd tell Selin, gently, that she might want to learn something with her hands, which she'd think was very funny coming from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only for the children. For myself, I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Selin think that's funny?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I spent her whole teenage years telling her to get off the farm and get an office job. Now I'd be telling her the office is the field and the field's the office. She'd say, Mum, make your mind up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever take that smartphone out of the drawer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, to see pictures of the grandchildren. Not for the farm. The farm doesn't need it, and by then the farm won't need me either.

S4.say: Ten years is fair enough and people have time to sort themselves out. I wouldn't make a fuss; I'll be on the bench outside the house by then.
S4.think: For me it's nearly the same as nothing happening. What bothers me is Selin, who'll be in her forties with a mortgage, doing a job a computer can do.
S4.do: Keeps farming as normal and stops at sixty-five as planned, perhaps keeping the orchard a little longer. Suggests to her daughter that she learn a practical, hands-on skill.
S4.feel: Uneasy for her children, but fine for herself.
S4.quote: Now I'd be telling her the office is the field and the field's the office.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Uma's own life is untouched, and her worry shifts completely to her daughter in accountancy. She sees the irony in having pushed Selin into an office job. The smartphone might finally come out, but only for grandchildren's photos.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. AGI by 2028. Hasan's job and my cows in the same year, and no time to think. What would help is a decent payoff for older workers like him, and a real person in the village to help with all the forms and changes, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who'll count the cows. A robot will count them right first time, I'm sure, but I like counting twice. It's the only bit of the day that's just me and them.

headlineQuote: A robot will count them right first time, I'm sure, but I like counting twice. It's the only bit of the day that's just me and them.
portrait: Uma Yilmaz, 58, runs a family hill farm with forty-two suckler cows and four acres of cider apples, mostly on her own while her husband Hasan drives a lorry for the farm merchant. She's pragmatic, not political, and resists anything new: her daughter's old smartphone sits in a drawer. The land is theirs and the savings are solid, so her fears are about purpose and her family rather than money. With two years' warning she'd sell the herd fast to avoid a price crash; with five or ten she'd say a slow goodbye, and her worry moves to her husband's job and her daughter's office work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her husband's lorry job and her cows would go in the same year with no time to think.
whatWouldHelp: A decent payoff for older workers like Hasan, and a real person in the village to help with forms and changes, not a website.
